Senses.Explanation: Something pounded into one continuous piece has no break between its former parts. Chan records apply this physical continuity image to twelve-period continuity and to paired fields—inner and outer, arising and perishing, motion and stillness, subject and object—while also recording an explicit denial that an iron-wall obstruction counts as one piece. Tianyin Yuanxiu says it must hold throughout the twelve periods of the day. Weian Deran predicates no separate arising or perishing mind and says motion and stillness are not two; Ruibai Mingxue predicates the disappearance of subject and object. Xiangyan says it took forty years. The Blue Cliff Record says the one-color side is also called being pounded into one piece, while Zhongfeng's Miscellaneous Record rejects equating it with a silver mountain and iron wall. Yulin Tongxiu's variant ‘struck into one piece’ joins walking, standing, sitting, lying, motion, stillness, leisure, and busyness; it is family evidence, not an exact-headword witness. The entry reports these text-drawn equations and rejections without supplying a theory that reconciles them.
Senses.Note: Seven exact witnesses across seven sources exceed the six-witness floor; the variant with ‘struck’ instead of ‘pounded’ is family evidence. Different paired terms—motion and stillness, arising and perishing, inner and outer, subject and object—are things said to become one piece, not different referents of the headword. No sense split is warranted.

Occurrences.Kwic: 自然打成一片。直得內心外境當下虛廓。彼聖此凡同時超越。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng Mingben, in the Extensive Record of Tianmu Zhongfeng (天目中峰廣錄), places being pounded into one piece after sustained continuity and says inner mind and outer objects open out while holy and ordinary are passed beyond.

Occurrences.Kwic: 十二時中須教打成一片，自無不辦之理。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Tianyin Yuanxiu, in the Recorded Sayings of Preceptor Tianyin (天隱和尚語錄), says it must be pounded into one piece throughout the twelve periods of the day.

Occurrences.Kwic: 打成一片，也無生的心，也無滅的心，生滅一如，動靜無二。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Weian Deran, in the Recorded Sayings of Preceptor Songyin Weian Ran (松隱唯菴然和尚語錄), predicates no separate arising or perishing mind and says motion and stillness are not two.

Occurrences.Kwic: 打成一片，情境俱亡，見色時不知色，聞聲時不知聲。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ruibai Mingxue, in the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Ruibai on Entering Office (入就瑞白禪師語錄), says that when pounded into one piece, subject and object both disappear.

Occurrences.Kwic: 行住坐臥動靜閒忙打作一片
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yulin Tongxiu, in the Recorded Sayings of National Teacher Puji Yulin (普濟玉琳國師語錄), uses the close variant ‘struck into one piece’ for walking, standing, sitting, lying, motion, stillness, leisure, and busyness.

Occurrences.Kwic: 老僧四十年方打成一片。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xiangyan Zhixian, quoted in the Collected Abridgment of Chan Master Guting's Sayings (古庭禪師語錄輯略), says that only after forty years was it pounded into one piece.

Occurrences.Kwic: 亦謂之普賢境界一色邊事。亦謂之打成一片。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu Keqin, in the Blue Cliff Record (佛果圜悟禪師碧巖錄), says that the one-color side of Samantabhadra's sphere is also called being pounded into one piece.

Occurrences.Kwic: 既知是銀山鐵壁，即不可謂之打成一片。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng Mingben, in the Miscellaneous Record of Chan Master Tianmu Mingben (天目明本禪師雜錄), rejects calling a known silver mountain and iron wall ‘pounded into one piece.’
